title: The Shape of Wanting
excerpt: Desire promises that the next thing will complete us. Usually it gives us a direction, a story, and another morning in which to revise both.
content:
Wanting is often described as a hole. We are missing something, so we reach. But some desires feel less like holes than windows. They show us a possible life and make the present rearrange itself around the view.

The trouble begins when the view hardens into a promise. We imagine the new job, the message, the recognition, and quietly ask it to deliver a self we can finally tolerate. The object changes; the bargain stays the same.

Still, I do not want to become suspicious of desire altogether. Wanting can be a form of attention. It tells us what has begun to matter, even when it gets the remedy wrong. The useful question is not how to want nothing, but what our wanting is trying to say before advertising and fear finish the sentence.

Some mornings the answer is embarrassingly small: more time, less noise, a walk without a destination. Small answers are not failures. They are often the first honest ones.
